Payroll Basics

Common payroll terminology

Payroll comes with its own vocabulary, and if you’re running payroll for the first time, you may encounter unfamiliar terms throughout the process.

This guide introduces some of the most common payroll terms you’ll see in payroll software, reports, and pay statements. Understanding these definitions can help you feel more confident as you learn the payroll process.

This page is intended as a general reference and explains common payroll concepts in plain language.

Payroll Basics

Payroll

Payroll is the process of calculating team member earnings, preparing team member payments, and maintaining records related to compensation. Payroll is typically completed on a recurring schedule, such as weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, or monthly.

Employer

An employer is the business or organization that hires and pays workers for the services they perform.

Employee

An employee is an individual who performs work under the hiring party’s direction and control and, unlike an independent contractor, is generally entitled to wages, employee benefits, and legal protections under applicable employment laws.

Independent Contractor

An independent contractor is a self-employed individual who provides services under a contract and, unlike a team member, controls how the work is performed and is not subject to the hiring party’s day-to-day direction or entitled to team member benefits.

Pay Cycle Terms

Pay Period

A pay period is the span of time during which team members earn wages before they are paid.

For example, a weekly pay period covers one week of work, while a biweekly pay period covers two weeks.

Payday

Payday is the date team members receive their pay for work completed during a pay period.

Many businesses establish recurring paydays so team members know when to expect payment.

Pay Schedule

A pay schedule determines how often payroll is processed and how frequently team members are paid.

Common pay schedules include weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, and monthly.

Earnings Terms

Gross Pay

Gross pay is a team member’s total earnings before deductions are applied.

Depending on the team member’s compensation, gross pay may include regular wages, overtime, bonuses, commissions, or other earnings.

Net Pay

Net pay is the amount a team member receives after payroll has accounted for applicable deductions.

Net pay is sometimes referred to as a team member’s “take-home pay.”

Salary

Salary is a fixed amount of compensation that is generally paid consistently regardless of the number of hours worked during a pay period.

Hourly Pay

Hourly pay is compensation based on the number of hours a team member works during a pay period.

Overtime

Overtime generally refers to additional compensation that may apply when eligible team members work beyond certain work hours.

Payroll systems calculate overtime separately from regular earnings.

Bonus

A bonus is additional compensation that an employer may provide in addition to a team member’s regular earnings.

Bonuses may be awarded for performance, company milestones, or other reasons.

Commission

A commission is compensation that is typically based on sales or other measurable performance.

Some team members receive commissions in addition to regular wages or salary.

Payroll Taxes

Employer Taxes

Taxes paid by the employer based on employee wages, in addition to the employee’s pay. Common examples include the employer’s share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, plus federal and state unemployment taxes.⁠⁠

Employee Taxes

Taxes withheld from an employee’s wages. Common examples include federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and applicable state and local taxes

Payroll Adjustments

Deduction

An amount subtracted from a team member’s gross pay during payroll. Deductions can include taxes, benefits, retirement contributions, and other payroll items, and together they determine the team member’s net pay.

Deductions are either:

  • Pre-tax: Taken out before taxes are calculated, which lowers the team member’s taxable income. Examples include health insurance premiums and traditional 401(k) contributions.
  • Post-tax: Taken out after taxes are calculated. Examples include wage garnishments and Roth 401(k) contributions.
Benefits Deduction

An amount taken from a team member’s pay for the benefits they’ve enrolled in, such as health insurance or a retirement plan. Benefits deductions can be pre-tax or post-tax, depending on the benefit, and appear on the team member’s pay statement.

Reimbursement

A reimbursement repays a team member for an approved business expense, separate from their regular earnings. Because a reimbursement isn’t wages, it isn’t taxed.

In Mercury, expense reimbursements are handled in Mercury banking* rather than through payroll.

Payment Terms

Direct Deposit

Direct deposit is an electronic method of delivering team member pay directly into a designated bank account.

Many employers choose direct deposit because it provides a convenient way to distribute team member payments.

Pay Stub

A pay stub is a summary that shows a team member’s earnings, deductions, and payment information for a specific pay period.

Team members often use their pay stub to review how their pay was calculated.

Payroll Records

Payroll Journal

A payroll journal summarizes payroll information for a payroll cycle.

Reports can provide an overview of team member earnings, deductions, and other payroll activity. In the absence of an accounting integration, your accountant can use a payroll journal to get the same information about payrolls.

Employee vs. independent contractor

Before someone begins working with our company, it’s important to understand whether they will be classified as an employee or an independent contractor (1099). This classification affects taxes, benefits, work expectations, and legal responsibilities.

What is an employee

An employee works under the direction and control of the company.

Typically, the company:

  • Sets work schedules and hours
  • Determines how work should be completed
  • Provides ongoing supervision and training
  • Supplies necessary tools and resources (when applicable)
  • Pays wages through payroll with taxes withheld

Employees may be:

  • Full-time
  • Part-time
  • Seasonal
Employees may receive
  • Health insurance
  • Paid time off (PTO)
  • Sick leave
  • Retirement benefits
  • Workers’ compensation coverage

What is an independent contractor (1099)?

An independent contractor is a self-employed professional who provides services for an agreed-upon project or time period.

Independent contractors control:

  • When they work
  • How they complete the work
  • Their own business operations

Contractors are responsible for paying their own taxes and generally do not receive employee benefits.

Examples include:

  • Consultants
  • Fractional service providers

Employee vs. contractor at a glance

Employee

Independent Contractor

Company controls work schedule

Sets own schedule

Company directs how work is completed

Decides how work is completed

Paid through payroll

Paid by invoice or contract

Taxes withheld by employer

Pays own taxes

Eligible for company benefits

Not eligible for employee benefits

Long-term employment relationship

Usually project-based or temporary

Receives a W-2

Completes a W-9 and typically receives a 1099-NEC

How worker classification is determined

The IRS determines whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor by considering the entire working relationship. No single factor determines classification.

1. Behavioral control

Who controls how the work gets done?

Examples include:

  • Instructions on how, when, or where to work
  • Required training
  • Direction on tools, equipment, or work methods
2. Financial control

Who controls the financial aspects of the work?

Examples include:

  • Investment in tools or equipment
  • Unreimbursed business expenses
  • Opportunity for profit or loss
3. Relationship between the parties

How do the worker and business view their relationship?

Examples include:

  • Written contracts
  • Employee benefits
  • Nature and length of the working relationship

The IRS considers all of these factors together when determining worker classification.

Taxforms

Employees

Complete:

  • Form W-4

Receive:

  • Form W-2 at year-end

Taxes are withheld from each paycheck.

Independent contractors

Complete:

  • Form W-9

May receive:

  • Form 1099-NEC for reportable compensation

Contractors are responsible for paying:

  • Federal income tax
  • Self-employment tax
  • Applicable state taxes

Risks of misclassification

Incorrectly classifying a worker can lead to:

  • IRS penalties
  • Back taxes
  • Wage and hour claims
  • Benefit disputes
  • Compliance issues

Worker classification should always be carefully evaluated using applicable federal, state, and local laws.

FAQs

Can a contractor set their own hours?

Yes. Independent contractors generally determine when and how they complete their work.

Do contractors receive company benefits?

No. Contractors typically are not eligible for employee benefits such as health insurance, paid time off, or retirement plans.

Who pays taxes for a contractor?

Independent contractors are responsible for paying their own federal, state, and self-employment taxes.

Can a contractor work for multiple companies?

Yes. Independent contractors are generally free to provide services to multiple clients.

Key takeaway

Choosing between an employee and an independent contractor depends on the nature of the work and the level of independence involved. Employees work under the company’s direction and receive wages and benefits through payroll. Independent contractors operate as self-employed professionals, control how they perform their work, and manage their own taxes and business operations.

When in doubt, consult Human Resources or a qualified legal or tax professional before determining worker classification.

Employer payroll taxes

Employer payroll taxes are taxes that employers are generally required to pay based on team member wages. These taxes help fund federal and state programs such as retirement benefits, Medicare, and unemployment insurance.

Unlike team member payroll tax withholdings (amounts withheld from a team member’s paycheck), employer payroll taxes are generally paid by the employer as an additional payroll expense.

Payroll tax requirements, rates, wage limits, and filing obligations can change and may vary based on federal, state, and local laws. This information is intended for educational purposes and should not be considered tax or legal advice.

Why employer payroll taxes exist

Employer payroll taxes help fund a variety of public programs, including:

  • Social insurance programs that support retirement, disability, and survivor benefits
  • Healthcare programs for eligible individuals
  • Unemployment insurance systems that provide temporary benefits to qualifying workers
  • Workforce development programs in certain states

Many of these programs are funded through contributions from both employers and team members, although funding requirements vary by tax and jurisdiction.

Common federal employer payroll taxes

1. Social security tax
  • Employer rate: Generally 6.2% of taxable wages
  • Wage base: Applies only up to the annual Social Security wage base, which is adjusted periodically
  • Purpose: Helps fund Social Security retirement, disability, and survivor benefits

In most situations, employers are required to contribute an amount equal to the team member’s Social Security tax.

2. Medicare tax
  • Employer rate: Generally 1.45% of all taxable wages
  • Wage base: No wage limit applies
  • Purpose: Helps fund the Medicare program

Employers generally match the team member Medicare tax. Team members with wages above certain federal thresholds may also owe an Additional Medicare Tax, which employers typically withhold but do not match.

3. Federal Unemployment Tax (FUTA)
  • Statutory rate: Generally 6.0% on the first $7,000 of taxable wages per team member
  • Potential effective rate: Many employers qualify for federal tax credits that may reduce the effective FUTA rate, although this can vary based on factors such as state unemployment tax payments and credit reduction status.
  • Purpose: Helps fund federal unemployment programs and support state unemployment systems

FUTA is generally paid by the employer and is not withheld from team member wages.

Common state employer payroll taxes

State payroll tax requirements vary by jurisdiction.

1. State Unemployment Insurance (SUI/UI)

State unemployment taxes generally help fund unemployment benefits.

Rates and wage bases may vary based on factors such as:

  • State law
  • Employer experience rating
  • Industry classification
  • Employer history

An employer’s unemployment tax rate may increase or decrease over time depending on applicable state rules.

2. Employment training tax

Some states impose additional employer payroll taxes that support workforce development or training programs.

For example, California currently assesses an Employment Training Tax (ETT) on certain employers, subject to state rules and annual wage limits.

3. Other state or local payroll taxes

Depending on the jurisdiction, employers may also be responsible for taxes or contributions related to:

  • State disability insurance programs
  • Paid family or medical leave programs
  • Local payroll taxes
  • Other employer-paid payroll assessments

Not all of these taxes apply in every state, and responsibility for payment may differ by program.

Summary

Employer payroll taxes vary based on several factors, including:

  • Business location: Federal taxes generally apply nationwide, while state and local payroll taxes vary by jurisdiction.
  • Team member wages: Some payroll taxes apply only up to an annual wage limit, while others apply to all taxable wages.
  • Employer tax rates: Certain taxes, such as state unemployment insurance, may use employer-specific rates that can change over time.
  • Applicable tax rules: Filing requirements, tax rates, wage bases, and available credits may change as laws and regulations are updated.

Because payroll tax requirements depend on the employer’s circumstances and applicable laws, the total employer payroll tax expense can vary from one business to another.

Team member payroll taxes

Team member payroll taxes are taxes that employers generally withhold from a team member’s wages and remit to the appropriate federal, state, or local tax authorities, as required by applicable law.

These withholdings help fund programs such as income taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and certain state or local programs.

Payroll tax requirements, withholding rules, tax rates, and wage limits may change over time and can vary by jurisdiction. This information is provided for educational purposes and should not be considered tax or legal advice.

Why team member payroll taxes exist

Team member payroll taxes help fund a variety of government programs and public services, including:

  • Income taxes → Government operations, infrastructure, and public services
  • Social Security → Retirement, disability, and survivor benefits
  • Medicare → Healthcare programs
  • State and local programs → Income taxes, disability insurance, paid leave, and other programs where applicable

Unlike employer payroll taxes, team member payroll taxes are generally withheld from a team member’s wages.

Common federal team member payroll taxes

1. Federal income tax

Federal income tax is generally withheld based on information the team member provides on Form W-4, along with applicable federal withholding rules.

The amount withheld may depend on factors such as:

  • Filing status
  • Multiple jobs
  • Dependents
  • Additional withholding elections
  • Other adjustments reflected on the team member’s Form W-4

The amount withheld is not necessarily the team member’s final federal income tax liability, which is generally determined when the team member files an annual tax return.

2. Social security tax
  • Team member rate: Generally 6.2% of taxable wages
  • Wage base: Applies up to the annual Social Security wage limit
  • Purpose: Helps fund retirement, disability, and survivor benefits

In most situations, employers contribute a matching amount.

3. Medicare tax
  • Team member rate: Generally 1.45% of taxable wages
  • Wage base: No wage limit applies
  • Purpose: Helps fund the Medicare program

Employers generally contribute a matching amount.

4. Additional medicare tax

Certain team members with wages above applicable federal thresholds may be subject to an Additional Medicare Tax.

Employers generally begin withholding this tax when required under federal rules. Unlike the standard Medicare tax, employers generally do not match this additional amount.

Common state and local team member payroll taxes

State and local payroll tax requirements vary by jurisdiction.

1. State income tax

Some states require employers to withhold state income tax from team member wages, while others do not.

Where applicable, withholding is generally based on state tax rules and team member withholding elections.

2. Local income taxes

Certain cities, counties, or other local jurisdictions may require additional payroll tax withholding.

Whether a local tax applies depends on the applicable laws where the team member works or resides.

3. State disability insurance (SDI)

Some states require team member payroll deductions to help fund state disability insurance programs.

Program availability, contribution requirements, and benefit rules vary by state.

4. Paid family leave (PFL)

Some jurisdictions fund paid family or medical leave programs through team member payroll deductions, employer contributions, or a combination of both.

Funding requirements vary by jurisdiction.

Things to keep in mind

Team member payroll tax withholding can vary based on several factors, including:

  • Federal, state, and local tax laws
  • Team member wages
  • Form W-4 and any applicable state withholding forms
  • Tax rates and wage limits
  • The team member’s work and residence locations
  • State or local payroll tax requirements

Payroll tax withholding is separate from other payroll deductions, such as retirement contributions, health insurance premiums, wage garnishments, or other voluntary or required deductions.

The amount withheld from a team member’s paycheck may not equal the team member’s final tax liability, which is generally determined when tax returns are filed.

Payroll Settings

Business updates that can impact payroll

Payroll runs on your company and team details. When something changes, payroll needs to know — and out of date details can mean incorrect withholding, errors on year-end tax documents, delayed payroll, or penalties from a state.

This article covers the changes that matter most for payroll and where to make each one.

1. Where your team works

Examples include:

  • Opening an office in a new state
  • Someone moving to a different state
  • Someone changing which office they work from

Why it matters: payroll taxes are based on where your team members work, not just where your business is registered. A move to a new state can change which taxes apply to someone and which jurisdictions Mercury files in.

Where to update it: add a work location in your payroll settings, and change someone’s work location on their profile. Work location changes go through a review that can take up to three business days. See Managing your payroll settings.

Let us know as soon as someone moves. If wages go unreported in a state, you may be subject to refiling costs and penalties.

2. Pay and compensation

Examples include:

  • Pay rate changes
  • Stipends, allowances, and recurring reimbursements
  • Wage garnishments and child support orders, including ones ordered by a court or state agency
  • Paying a group of people on a different frequency

Why it matters: accurate pay details keep your team paid correctly and payroll taxes calculated properly.

Where to update it: on the person’s profile, under Manage pay. See Managing someone’s payroll details.

To pay a group on a different frequency, add a new pay schedule and move them to it — a schedule’s frequency can’t be changed once it’s created. See Understanding pay schedules.

3. Team member details

Examples include:

  • Address changes
  • Legal name changes
  • Social Security number corrections
  • Tax withholding changes, including claiming an exemption

Why it matters: these feed directly into withholding and year-end tax documents, so out of date details cause incorrect withholding and errors on a W-2.

Where to update it depends on the detail:

  • Most details — from the Team section of your Payroll home page. Select the person’s name to view and edit certain details
  • Social Security number corrections — contact support
  • Home address — contact support from the the team member’s details page under “Personal”
  • Tax withholding — team members change their own from their “My Payroll” page, and re-sign the updated form. See What team members see during payroll onboarding

4. Your company’s legal details

Examples include:

  • Changing your entity type, such as converting from an LLC to an S Corp
  • Receiving a new EIN
  • Changing your company’s legal name or address
  • Changes in ownership, including adding or removing partners
  • Closing or selling part of your business

Why it matters: these affect how your payroll taxes are filed and reported, and incorrect entity information can result in refiling fees.

Where to update it: contact support. These details come from your Mercury account and can’t be changed in your payroll settings. Get in touch before the change takes effect where you can.

5. Your payroll funding account

Examples include:

  • Changing which Mercury account funds payroll
  • Closing the account payroll is paid from

Why it matters: payroll is debited from this account, so keeping it current prevents failed debits and delayed payments to your team.

Where to update it: your “Pay schedules” page in payroll settings. See Managing your payroll settings.

If you’re not sure

If you’re not sure whether a change affects payroll, get in touch before you make it. It’s easier to sort out in advance than to correct a filing afterwards.

The same goes for anything official you receive about payroll taxes — contact support as soon as it arrives, since these usually carry deadlines.

Managing your payroll settings

Your payroll settings are where you manage your pay schedules, payroll funding account, work locations, state tax details, and signatories.

This article covers how to find your payroll settings and what you can manage in each section.

Open your payroll settings

  • Go to your Payroll home page
  • Select Settings
  • Select the setting you want to manage from the left-hand menu of your dashboard on web

Pay schedules

The Pay schedules page lists each pay schedule you’ve set up, including:

  • How often the schedule runs
  • The next payday
  • How many people are on the schedule
  • Whether payroll is submitted manually or automatically

You can create multiple pay schedules when different team members or types of pay need to be paid on different timelines. For example, you might use a separate schedule for:

  • Hourly team members whose payday falls after the end of their pay period
  • Team members who are subject to different pay frequency requirements
  • Stipends or other additional pay that you pay on a different schedule from regular wages

You’re responsible for choosing pay schedules that meet applicable wage and hour requirements.

Select Add pay schedule to create a new schedule.

Select an existing schedule to view its details, edit its name, or move members off one pay schedule onto a new one. You’ll also see a preview of your next pay run. Learn more here.

Payroll funding account

Your payroll funding account is the Mercury account used to pay your payroll. You can view or change it from the Pay schedules page. External bank accounts aren’t supported.

This account is also used for benefits registration and shared with your workers’ compensation vendor. Changing it also updates the funding account for benefits vendors managed by Mercury or Central, except 401(k) and Thatch.

Make sure the account has enough funds to cover payroll to help prevent failed debits and associated fees.

Work locations

The Work locations page lists the addresses your team works from and the number of team members assigned to each location. Work locations determine which payroll tax jurisdictions Mercury files in and the taxes your team members pay.

Select Add work location to add another location.

Please notify us as soon as team members move to new workplaces, you may be subject to refiling costs and penalties from states if you fail to report wages.

Tax accounts

Your Tax accounts page hold your state payroll tax registrations, grouped by state. For each state your team works in, you’ll find:

  • Accounts & IDs — your withholding and unemployment account numbers for that state. Select the eye icon to reveal a number
  • Rates — expand to see the tax rates that apply to you
  • Elections — expand to see your tax elections

Signatories

The Signatory page list the company members who are authorized to sign on behalf of your company. A signatory must complete payroll setup and tax authorizations.

Select Change signatory to make a change. Signatories must have a signature on file. If you select someone who doesn’t have one, they’ll be prompted to add their signature before you can add them as a signatory.

Only eligible company members appear when you add a signatory. If the person you want to add isn’t listed, add them as a company member first.

Frequently asked questions

Can I edit a work location?

You can edit a work location until wages have been paid to someone working at that location. After wages have been paid, the address can’t be changed. If the address is incorrect or changes, add a new work location and move the relevant team members to it.

How do work locations work for remote team members?

A remote team member’s home address is their work location. Individual home addresses don’t appear in the company’s work location list, which shows office locations.

If multiple team members work from the same home, you can add that address as a company work location and assign them to it.

How do I move someone to a different work location?

Change a team member’s work location from their individual profile via Payroll home > Team section. Changes to work locations go through a review process and may take up to 3 business days.

Understanding pay schedules

A pay schedule determines when your team is paid, which dates each pay period covers, and when payroll needs to be submitted. Every pay run is tied to a pay schedule.

This article covers what a pay schedule includes, how to add one, and what you can change after it’s created.

What a pay schedule includes

Each pay schedule defines:

  • How often your team is paid
  • When each pay period starts and ends
  • The payday
  • Whether payroll is submitted automatically or manually

You’ll create your first pay schedule during payroll setup, when you choose a pay frequency and your first payday.

Choosing a pay frequency

Your pay frequency determines how often people on the schedule are paid as well as how taxes are calculated on each paycheck. Mercury offers:

  • Weekly — 52 paydays a year
  • Every two weeks — 26 paydays a year
  • Twice a month — 24 paydays a year, such as the 15th and last day of the month
  • Monthly — 12 paydays a year
  • Quarterly — 4 paydays a year
  • Annually — 1 payday a year

Mercury shows the number of paydays for each frequency and previews upcoming paydays before you create the schedule.

You’re responsible for choosing pay schedules that meet applicable wage and hour requirements.

Adding a pay schedule

To add a pay schedule:

  • From your homepage, head to Settings > Pay schedules
  • Select Add pay schedule
  • Enter a name that describes who’s on the schedule, like “Contractors (weekly)”
  • Choose a pay frequency
  • Set the first payday and the end of the first pay period
  • Select Create schedule

Automatic and manual submission

Each pay schedule can be set to submit automatically or manually. Your first pay schedule uses auto-submit by default. If you prefer to submit payroll yourself, change the submission setting on the Pay schedules page.

  • Auto-submit — Mercury creates each pay run and submits it at the deadline without you taking any action
  • Manual — Mercury creates each pay run, and you submit it yourself

With auto-submit, payroll is submitted whether or not you’ve reviewed the pay run. Make sure any changes to someone’s pay are entered before the submission deadline.

Changing a pay schedule

Select a schedule from the “Pay schedules” page to open its details. You’ll see its next payday, pay frequency, and who’s paid on the schedule.

From there, you can:

  • Select Edit name to rename the schedule
  • Select Move members to move people to another schedule
  • Select More to switch between auto-submit and manual submission, make the schedule your primary schedule, or disable it

You can’t change a schedule’s pay frequency after it’s created. To pay a group on a different frequency, add a new schedule and move them to it.

You also can’t disable your primary schedule. Set another schedule as primary first.

Note: You can’t delete a pay schedule once someone has been paid through it.

Using more than one pay schedule

Most companies use a single pay schedule. You might add another when a group of people needs a different pay frequency or timing, such as:

  • Hourly team members who submit their hours before being paid, with payday falling a few days after the pay period ends
  • Team members in a state with a more frequent pay requirement
  • A stipend paid on a different cadence from regular wages

For stipends, you may also be able to prorate the amount across your regular pay periods instead of creating another schedule.

Each pay schedule runs independently, with its own frequency, paydays, and submission setting.

FAQs

Can I change the pay frequency of an existing schedule?

No. A pay schedule’s frequency can’t be changed after the schedule is created. To use a different frequency, create a new pay schedule and move the relevant people to it.

Can I disable a pay schedule?

Yes, unless it’s your primary schedule. To disable your primary schedule, first make another schedule your primary one.

Can I move someone to a different pay schedule?

Yes. Open the schedule they’re currently on and select Move members to move them to another schedule.

People & Access

Adding your clients to Mercury Books

If you’re an accountant or bookkeeper working with Mercury clients, you can use Mercury Books to do their bookkeeping. This article explains how to get a client set up and what to expect once you’re in.

Getting a client started

Before an advisor can access Mercury Books, the client themselves must subscribe to the product. Adding a new subscription can only be managed by an admin of the Mercury organization. An advisor will not be able to access Books until this is done.

  • If the client is not yet subscribed to Mercury Books, they must do so by by selecting “Books” from the main navigation, clicking “Create your Books” button on the landing page, and accepting the new subscription and associated fees
  • The client invites you into their Mercury organization with a role that includes the Books permissions

Guiding a client through setup

During initial setup, the client determines the basic configurations for Mercury Books. There are three things worth advising them on and getting right up front:

  • Accounting basis: cash or accrual. This is set at creation, and not easily modifiable after the fact without contacting support and rebuilding the books. See our Requesting a change to your accounting basis or chart of accounts article
  • Chart of accounts. If you have a standard template you like to use, provide it to your client as a CSV so that they can upload it during onboarding, instead of using the Books default chart of accounts.
  • Connected accounts. Mercury banking and credit card accounts will be automatically integrated but any third party accounts must be connected. This includes non-Mercury banking and credit card accounts, as well as integrations to payroll or payment processors as required.

Accessing a client’s books

Open your client list in the Advisor Portal and click the Books icon next to the client’s name. This brings you into their organization and opens Books.

To move between clients, use the Switch Books section of the org menu.

Note: Mercury Books supports working in one client’s books at a time. To have two clients open simultaneously, use separate browser profiles or an incognito window.

Permissions you’ll need

Your role in the client’s organization needs the all accounts, accounting, invoice creation, and recipient management permissions. The client can set all four by turning on the Mercury Books toggle when creating or editing your role.

If you hit an error opening Books or matching a payment, this is almost always the cause. See our Sharing access to your books article.

FAQs

Can I set up Books on behalf of my client?

Your client needs to subscribe to Books and grant you access to their Mercury organization first. Once you’re in with the right permissions, you can drive setup.

Can I use one chart of accounts template across clients?

Yes. Share your desired chart of accounts with your client and they can import it during setup. You can also update the chart of account after the fact in Books.

Can I migrate a client’s history from QuickBooks Online?

Not automatically. Plan a period cutover — see our Moving to Books from another accounting software article.

How do I get a client’s basis or chart of accounts changed after setup?

Contact support. See our Requesting a change to your accounting basis or chart of accounts article.

Requesting a change to your accounting basis or chart of accounts

Two setup decisions in Mercury Books — your accounting basis and the overall structure of your chart of accounts — are made when your books are created. Changing either one after the fact is something we handle for you. This article explains what you can change yourself, what to ask for, and what to expect.

What you can change yourself

Before requesting anything, it’s worth knowing what’s already in your hands on the Chart of Accounts page:

  • Add an account. Click the + button and enter a code, name, and type
  • Rename an account. Open the row, edit the name, and save. The change applies everywhere, including to transactions already coded to it
  • Change an account code. Renumber accounts to match your preferred convention
  • Delete an account. Open it and delete. An account with line entries posted to it can’t be deleted — recategorize those transactions first
  • Move transactions between accounts. Filter the Transactions page and recategorize in bulk

To do this more easily, you can also request certain chart of accounts changes via Command. For more information, see our Understanding your chart of accounts article.

Note: System ledgers can’t be renamed, renumbered, or deleted.

When to request a change

Contact support when you need one of these:

  • A different accounting basis. Switching your books from cash to accrual or accrual to cash. We support a one-time change.
  • A replacement chart of accounts. A wholesale replacement of your chart of accounts, and for all historical transactions to be automatically categorized according to this new set. This is typically a template that should replace what you have rather than sit alongside it.

What to expect after requesting a change

Both changes rebuild your books on the new setting and recategorize your transactions against it. That means:

  • Your journal entries are recreated on the new basis or against the new accounts
  • Your transactions are recategorized, and will need review afterward
  • Your reconciliations need to be redone
  • Manual journal entries you’ve made — opening balances, accruals, adjustments — should be checked and in some cases re-entered

It’s effectively re-onboarding your books, which is why it’s worth making the change as early as you can.

Tip: Before you request a change, export the reports you’ll want to compare against afterward. Go to Reports, set your period, and export to XLSX.

Making the request

Contact support and tell us:

  • Which change you need — a basis change, a chart of accounts replacement, or both
  • For a basis change, which basis you want to move to
  • For a chart of accounts replacement, attach the chart of accounts you want to use

Deciding whether to change

Whether your books should be on cash or accrual, and how your chart of accounts should be structured, are accounting judgments rather than product questions. We can’t advise on either — talk to a qualified accountant or bookkeeper first, then come to us with what you need.

FAQs

Can I switch my basis more than once?

We support a one-time change. If you’re not certain which basis you want, settle it with your accountant before requesting the switch.

Will I lose my transactions?

No. Your transactions stay. What changes is how they’re recorded and categorized, which is why review afterward matters.

How long does it take?

We’ll confirm timing when you reach out, and let you know when it’s done so you can review.

Can I add a batch of accounts without replacing my whole chart of accounts?

Yes. Accounts are added one at a time from the Chart of Accounts page. If you have a longer list, use Command which can manage bulk changes.

Sharing access to your books

Access to Mercury Books is granted through your Mercury team roles rather than a separate user list inside Books. Anyone on your team whose role includes the required permissions can access Books. This article explains how to manage that access.

What Books requires

What you can do in Books is controlled by four permissions:

  • All accounts — required. Books covers every account in your organization, so partial account access causes errors
  • Accounting — required
  • Invoice creation — required for payment matching
  • Recipient management — needed for modifying vendor records

You need both All accounts and Accounting permissions to open Books. Without Invoice creation or Recipient management, you can still access Books, but the related features won’t be available.

Adding your accountant to your team

  • Click your company name in the top left corner of your dashboard
  • Go to Settings > Team
  • Invite a new team member with their email address
  • Assign them a role with Mercury Books enabled
  • Send the invite

Once they accept, Books appears in their sidebar.

Adding Books access to a new or existing role

Roles have a Mercury Books toggle that selects all four permissions at once.

  • Click your company name in the top left corner of your dashboard
  • Go to Settings > Team
  • Click the Roles tab
  • Create a new role, or open an existing one to edit
  • Turn on Mercury Books
  • Click Save role

The toggle turns itself off if you deselect any of the four permissions, so it always reflects the role’s actual state.

Giving access to a bookkeeping firm

A firm you work with accesses your books through their Advisor Portal, which brings them into your account. They still need a role in your Mercury organization with the Books permissions.

See our Working with a bookkeeper in Mercury Books article.

What someone with access can see

Everything in your books — all transactions, all accounts, all reports. Books doesn’t have permissions within it, so access is all or nothing.

If you only want to share your financial statements, export the reports instead. Go to Reports, set the period, and export to XLSX. That’s often the right approach for someone who only needs statements at year end.

Removing access

Remove the team member from Settings > Users, or move them to a role without the Books permissions. Either removes their access to your books.

FAQs

Can I give someone read-only access to Books?

Not currently. Export the reports they need instead.

Can I limit someone to just the reports page?

No. Access to Books covers every screen in it.

Can I give someone access to Books but not my banking?

You can build a role that includes the Books permissions without send-money permissions, so they can work in your books without moving money. Note that Books requires visibility into all of your accounts.

My accountant can’t match payments.

Their role is likely missing the invoice creation permission. Turn on the Mercury Books toggle on their role to set all four at once.

How many people can have access?

There’s no limit. Anyone on your team with a role that includes the Books permissions can open your books.

Working with a bookkeeper in Mercury Books

Mercury Books works whether you handle your books yourself, work with a bookkeeper you already have, or want to be introduced to one. This article explains each path, how a bookkeeper gets access to your books, and how to change your mind later.

The three paths

After signing up for Books, you will be presented with one of three ways to use the product, and none of them is permanent:

  • Get matched with a bookkeeper. Mercury introduces you to a partner bookkeeping firm suited to your business.
  • Bring your own bookkeeper. You invite the bookkeeper or accountant you already work with into your Mercury account, and they work in your books alongside you.
  • Do it yourself. You categorize transactions, create journal entries, reconcile your accounts, and pull your own reports. Plenty of founders run Books this way.

Getting matched with a bookkeeper

If you’d like to work with an accountant or bookkeeper, but don’t have one, Mercury can match you with a partner bookkeeping firm, based on the needs of your business.

When the match is made, we email you an introduction to the firm, copying them and your Mercury partner manager so you have a point of contact on our side. This process typically takes 1 - 2 business days.

Note: This matching service is an introduction only; partner firms set their own pricing, and you pay the firm directly. Bookkeeping services aren’t included with Mercury Books — what’s included is the software. Ask about pricing and scope when the firm reaches out.

Bringing your own bookkeeper

During setup you either select someone already on your Mercury team or invite someone new.

To select an existing team member:

  • Choose them from the list of team members
  • If their role doesn’t include the permissions Books needs, you’ll be prompted to either move them to an eligible role or add Books permissions to the role they’re on

To invite someone new:

  • Enter their email address and choose a role for them
  • If the role you picked doesn’t include the permissions Books needs, you’ll be prompted to update it
  • Send the invite

Once they accept, they can open Books from your Mercury dashboard. If an invite doesn’t go through or lapses, you can reassign the bookkeeper from your setup screen.

Note: A bookkeeper needs the all accounts, accounting, invoice creation, and recipient management permissions. The Mercury Books toggle on a role selects all four at once. See our Sharing access to your books article.

What your bookkeeper sees

A bookkeeping firm opens your books through their Advisor Portal by clicking Open Books in the Open next to your name in their client list, which brings them into your account.

Changing your mind

The path you choose at setup isn’t locked in.

Do I need a bookkeeper to use Books?

No. Books is built to work whether you want to manage your books yourself or hire a professional.

Can I work with more than one bookkeeper?

Yes. Anyone on your Mercury team with the right permissions can work in your books.

Creating single use cards on Mercury Personal

Single-use cards are rolling out incrementally. Stay tuned for general availability.

Single-use cards are virtual debit cards that automatically close after one approved purchase. They’re useful for one-time transactions and may help reduce the risk of unauthorized charges from unfamiliar merchants.

This article explains how to create a single-use card and what happens after you’ve used it.

Create a single-use card

You can create single-use cards from your Mercury dashboard on web.

  • Go to your Cards page
  • Click Create card
  • Select a Cardholder and enter a Card nickname
  • Under “Type,” select Virtual
  • Under “Usage (optional),” check Single-use
  • Configure any additional settings, including spend controls, as needed
  • Click Create card

How single-use cards work

A single-use card automatically closes after its first approved purchase over $0. Once closed, its status changes to Used, and it can’t be reopened.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • Declined transactions and $0 authorization checks won’t count as a purchase, so your card will remain active
  • You can still receive refunds on a used card or dispute a transaction as you normally would
  • Since the card can only be used once, avoid using it for ongoing subscriptions or free trials
  • Charges submitted without an authorization request (known as “force posts”) can still be processed, even if your single-use card has already been used or is past its custom expiration date. If the card hasn’t been used yet, the transaction will mark it as used and close it.

If you need to make another payment, you can create a new single-use or standard card.

How to dispute a Mercury Personal transaction

If you see a charge you don’t recognize or you’re unable to resolve an issue with a merchant, you may be able to dispute the transaction directly from your Mercury account. This article explains which transactions are eligible and how to submit a dispute.

What types of transactions can be disputed?

You can dispute debit card and ACH pull transactions directly from your Mercury dashboard or the iOS app (make sure you’re using the latest version).

To be eligible, the transaction must be fully processed. This means:

  • The transaction is no longer pending
  • The funds have left your account

Pending, canceled, or failed transactions can’t be disputed. If you’re concerned about unauthorized activity, freeze your card right away to prevent additional charges while the transaction settles.

The following transactions aren’t eligible for self-service disputes:

  • Internal transfers between your Mercury accounts
  • Wire transfers
  • Other non-card or non-ACH transaction types

If you’re disputing a non-USD fraudulent transaction, we’ll also return the currency conversion fee.

If you need help with a transaction that isn’t eligible for self-service or have questions, contact our support team.

Disputing a fraudulent or unauthorized transaction

First, freeze your card through the Mercury dashboard. This will prevent further charges from going through if you suspect fraud.

Then do the following:

  • Go to your Transactions page
  • Find the transaction you want to dispute and click on it to open the transaction details
  • Click on the three dots icon in the bottom right of the transaction details card, and select Dispute Transaction
  • We’ll ask you a few questions and give you a chance to provide any additional info or documentation
  • Once you submit, our team will review the dispute and email you back with an update within a few business days. Depending on the outcome, they’ll be able to cancel and reissue cards as needed and get the fraudulent charges cleared up

Disputing an authorized charge with a merchant or service provider

If you recognize the charge but have an issue with the product or service, we recommend contacting the merchant first.

Merchant disputes and chargebacks can take up to 90 days to reach a resolution, as the merchant is required by law to be given “ample time” to respond. Because of this, you might find a faster resolution by working with them directly.

If the merchant is unresponsive or unwilling to help, follow the steps above to dispute the charge and provide as much information as possible, including screenshots of your attempts to contact the merchant.

Disputing an international wire

If there was an error with an international wire sent from your personal account, you are able to dispute it within 180 days of delivery. Learn about wire disputes and cancellations here.

Personal Debit Card FAQs

What’s the difference between a virtual card and a physical card?

Physical debit cards are shipped to you via USPS. These debit cards can be used anywhere that accepts Mastercard.

Virtual debit cards are unique cards with no physical counterpart that have their own card numbers, expiration date, and CVC code. Virtual debit cards can be created at any time from the Cards page of your Mercury dashboard and can be used immediately.

Virtual debit cards can be used to make online transactions anywhere that accepts Mastercard, and are a great option if you need to make purchases while you wait for a physical card to arrive.

What are the fees associated with using a Mercury debit card?

We don’t charge any transaction fees for use of your Mercury debit card. This applies to both U.S. domestic and international transactions.

If you use your debit card to purchase something in a non-USD currency, MasterCard will set its own conversion rate. You can get a rough idea of MasterCard’s conversion rates here.

Does Mercury charge ATM fees to withdraw money?

Mercury doesn’t charge fees to withdraw money, but some ATM networks might. If the ATM network charges a fee, it will be displayed prior to withdrawing your funds so you can decide whether or not you want to proceed.

Does Mercury offer cash withdrawal at the point of sale?

Yes, you can withdraw cash at the point of sale using your physical or virtual card. Keep in mind that cashback withdrawals count toward your daily transaction and ATM withdrawal limits.

Do you offer cash deposits on Mercury debit cards?

Not currently.

Can I send Instant Payouts to my Mercury debit card?

Yes! Instant Payouts sometimes experience slight delays that are dependent on the card processors, but the transfer will be completed within a few hours and is much faster than sending an ACH or wire to your account.

What countries will Mercury debit cards not work in?

You can see a full list of where we prohibit card usage in this article.

What does it mean if I have a pending transaction in my card activity?

A “pending” card transaction means the merchant either hasn’t fully authorized the payment or it hasn’t completed the payment failure yet.

We give merchants 30 business days to process or cancel the payment before we manually cancel it.

If you’re seeing a pending amount that’s greater than your purchase, this is a pre-authorization. These charges remain pending for a few business days before they either settle for the correct amount or fall off of the account.

The Mercury Debit Cards are issued by Choice Financial Group and Column N.A., Members FDIC, pursuant to licenses from Mastercard®.

Processing times for card transactions

When you make a purchase with your Mercury Debit card, the transaction might not settle right away. This article explains why you might see a charge marked as “pending” and how long it typically takes to settle.

Why a transaction is pending

Pending transactions happen because card payments go through card networks, which allow merchants to pre-authorize payments. A pending charge means the merchant has started a transaction but hasn’t fully processed it yet.

Common reasons for pending charges:

  • The merchant hasn’t finished authorizing or declining the payment
  • The transaction is pre-authorized but not yet finalized
  • The merchant is still reconciling their books

How long it takes for transactions to settle

Most transactions settle or cancel within 1–3 business days, though some may settle immediately. Merchants have up to 30 business days to process or cancel a payment. If they don’t take action within that time, we’ll manually cancel the pending charge.

Why a pending charge might be higher than your purchase

Some merchants place a pre-authorization hold on your card for more than your actual purchase amount. This is common with gas stations, hotels, car rental companies, When you make a purchase with your Mercury Debit or IO Credit card, the transaction doesn’t settle right away. This article explains why you might see a charge marked as “pending” and how long it typically takes to settle.

By creating a merchant-locked card or adding a merchant lock to an existing virtual card, be advised that this action does not nullify any existing contract between you and additional merchants. A merchant may still have the ability to force post and bypass our authorization. You must directly contact any additional merchant to update your card number or cancel your subscription.

Set or edit limits for your Mercury Personal debit card

If you’re an admin or account holder, you can easily adjust the spending limit of any debit cards associated with your Mercury Personal account. This allows you to keep a tighter control on spending and stick to daily or monthly budgets.

Here’s how to do it:

  • Go to your Cards page.
  • Click on the card with the limit you would like to edit to open the card details.
  • Click More, then select Edit Limit.
  • You can select a daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, on a permanent or temporary basis depending on the needs of your business. Daily limits give you more granular control, while monthly limits are a little more flexible.

If you’re planning a purchase that requires a limit higher than the dashboard allows, please email personal@mercury.com with an invoice or contract representing the larger purchase. We’ll review your request to determine whether we can raise the card limit to that amount.

Cash withdrawal limits

You can use your Mercury Personal debit card at ATMs to withdraw up to $3,000 cash per card per business day, with a maximum daily withdrawal limit of $3,000 across all cardholders on the account. Cashback withdrawals also count toward your daily transaction and ATM withdrawal limits.

Example: If you have 3 cardholders on your Mercury account and 1 of them withdraws $3,000 in a single business day, the other cardholders would not be able to withdraw any additional funds until the next day. They still have a $3,000 individual withdrawal limit, but it gets superseded by the overall account withdrawal limit

When do limits reset?

Card limit windows always begin at the same time, even if they are temporary.

  • Daily limits begin at 12:00 am UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and last for 24 hours.
  • Weekly limits start on Sunday 12:00 am UTC and last for 7 days.
  • Monthly limits start at the 1st of the month at 12:00 am UTC and last through the end of the calendar month.

Example: If you update your limit to monthly on September 15th, your new monthly spending limit would be in effect for the remainder of September and reset again on Oct 1st. Going forward, the limit will continue to reset on the 1st of each month. This is true for daily and weekly limits as well.

Adjusting your limits does not change how much you’ve previously spent in a period. For example: If you start the week with a limit of $100/day and spend $100 on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, you would have spent $300 for the week. On Wednesday, if you set a limit of $300/week, you won’t be able to spend until next week because you’ve already used up the limit for that period.

Note: ATM limits reset on business days, so withdrawals may be declined if you hit your limit over weekends or holidays.

Setting a temporary daily, weekly, or monthly limit will always take into account the money you’ve spent within the set period. If on a Wednesday you set a temporary weekly limit for the next seven days, this temporary weekly limit will still reset on Sunday at 12:00 am UTC.

If a charge exceeds your limit

Card limits are meant to help control spending and not prevent good-faith transactions from a merchant. In that spirit, there are a few legitimate reasons a merchant may be able to process a charge on your Mercury card above the limit you’ve set.

  • Recurring Charge or Subscription: Recurring charges are usually subscription-based. If the merchant was authorized to charge you with the initial debit, this authorization persists even if you alter your limits. In these cases, we recommend contacting the merchant to cancel the recurring payment - you can always re-authorize with them at a later date by re-signing up.
  • Force Posts: This occurs when a merchant uses a previous authorization code to push through a transaction. Governments and utilities use force posts most commonly, but they can also be used to refund money back to a canceled card.
  • Pre-authorizations: Similar to recurring charges (because technically the recurring charges are all pre-authorized). The debit card infrastructure allows a merchant to change the final charged amount by up to 20% before it’s automatically blocked. Think about paying at the pump or using a delivery service that charges an initial amount and then updates it to reflect tax or tips.

Regardless, if you believe a transaction is incorrect or fraudulent, we can help you resolve the situation.

Understanding your 1099-INT tax forms

If you earned $10 or more in interest or signup bonuses from Mercury in a calendar year, you’ll receive one or more 1099 tax forms. This article explains which forms you might receive and where to find them.

Where to find your tax forms

All tax documents will be available in Documents & Data > Tax Documents in your Mercury dashboard. Some forms will be available starting January 31, 2026. All forms will be issued no later than February 17, 2026.

What forms you might receive

1099-INT

You’ll receive a 1099-INT form if you earned $10 or more in interest in 2025 from your Mercury account(s) and/or you received a signup bonus through a Mercury referral link.

Details:

  • If you have both an individual and joint Mercury account and earned $10+ in each, you’ll get separate 1099-INTs for each account
  • Similarly, if you have accounts with separate partner banks, you’ll receive a 1099-INT for each
  • Signup bonuses will appear on a separate 1099-INT form with Mercury listed as the payer
  • For joint accounts, the form is issued to the primary account holder only
  • For revocable trust accounts with multiple grantors, Mercury uses a designated primary grantor for tax reporting and 1099 issuance purposes.

Reminder: No 1099-INT will be issued if you earned less than $10 in total interest from an account in 2025. If you believe you should have received one, please reach out to peronal@mercury.com.

1099 Consolidated

You’ll receive a 1099 Consolidated form if you used Invest in the previous calendar year and received dividends or realized returns. This form includes all relevant tax reporting for your investments.

1099-MISC

You’ll receive a 1099-MISC form with Mercury listed as the payer if you earned $600 or more in referral bonuses in 2025.

Mercury does not provide tax advice. If you have questions about your trust structure or tax reporting obligations, consult a qualified tax professional.

What if my account was closed or suspended?

Why you’re seeing two Invest statements (June 2026) (Personal: Documents & Data)

If you have a Mercury Invest account, you may notice something a little different this month: two emails and two June statements in your Documents & Data folder. This is expected due to a transition to a more robust backend platform. There is no action needed from you.

What’s happening

We’re migrating Mercury Invest to a more modern infrastructure. Both the old and new systems generated a statement for June, which is why you’re seeing two.

You don’t need to do anything. One statement reflects the monthly activity before the transition and the other reflects the activity post transition.

What’s changing

Mercury Advisory continues to use Apex as the custodian. We’re not changing who holds your investments.

What we are upgrading is the underlying platform from Apex Classic to Apex Ascend. This is a backend change that lays the groundwork for new features and a better Invest experience going forward.

This migration is not a taxable event. No assets are being sold or transferred, and there are no tax consequences as a result of this change.

How Mercury uses AI in Command (Personal: Getting Started)

Mercury Command is powered by AI and designed to complete financial work for you. It retrieves information, stages actions, and executes — with your confirmation as the final step before anything changes in your account.

When you use Command, nothing ever happens without your explicit approval.

The AI’s role

When you send a message in Command, the AI interprets what you’re asking, retrieves the relevant information from your account, and prepares a response or stages an action for you to review.

The AI does the legwork — finding the right transactions, pre-filling the right fields, surfacing the right details — so that by the time you see a result, all you need to do is confirm or adjust.

Every Command response links directly to the underlying transaction, invoice, or account data behind it so you can verify the source before you act.

What the AI can see

Command authenticates through your existing Mercury session. This means it can only access the data and actions a user is already authorized to see and take in their Mercury account. There is no elevated access — if you can’t do something in the Mercury web or mobile product, Command can’t do it either.

The context shared with the AI for each session is limited by design. It includes basic session information like your first name, business name, and timezone. It does not include session cookies, authentication secrets, or API keys.

What the AI never sees

Sensitive personal and financial data is not transmitted to the AI model. This includes:

  • Card numbers
  • Social Security numbers
  • Dates of birth
  • Home addresses

When Command needs to reference something sensitive — like a card number — it passes the model a reference ID instead of the real data. The Mercury interface handles the conversion, so you see what you need to see, but the underlying data never passed through the AI.

Third-party AI providers

Mercury Command is powered by third-party AI providers. Some account data is shared with these providers to generate responses. Your conversations are not used to train their models, and sensitive financial data is never transmitted to them.

All AI vendors that power Mercury products go through a thorough security and privacy review before we engage them, and are contractually prohibited from using your data for any purpose beyond providing services to Mercury — including training their own models. We also review vendors on an ongoing basis to ensure they continue to meet our standards.

Every action requires your confirmation

Command can retrieve information and stage actions, but it cannot execute anything without your explicit approval. Before anything happens in your account, Command shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for you to confirm. You can also edit what’s been staged before approving.

There is no auto-approve under any circumstances.

AI features in Mercury are entirely optional. Your core account features — payments, cards, and account management — work exactly the same if you choose not to use Command.

Mercury Command overview (Personal: Getting Started)

Mercury Command is a conversational interface built directly into your Mercury account. Instead of navigating between pages and dashboards, you can type what you need in plain language to get answers and take action — from checking your cash position to sending a payment to updating a card limit.

What you can do with Command

Command works across the products already in your Mercury account. You can:

  • Ask questions — check balances, find transactions, view account details and statements. Every answer is drawn from your live account data
  • Take action — send payments, freeze cards, categorize transactions, create and send invoices, and more. Command stages every action for your review first and does not execute until you confirm
  • Edit settings — update card limits, auto-transfer rules, user permissions, and similar account settings without navigating between pages
  • Verify responses — every answer links directly to the underlying transaction, invoice, or account data so you can check the source
  • Reach support — escalate any conversation and get routed to a real person on our support team without leaving the chat

Command can only perform actions that are already available to you in Mercury. It does not have elevated permissions. For example, if you have a monthly spend limit on your account, Command cannot override that permission. Every action is bound by these existing permissions and governed by the same approval policies and risk controls that protect your Mercury account.

How confirmation works

Command never takes action without your explicit approval. When you ask it to do something, it stages the action — pre-filling the details and showing you exactly what will happen — and stops. Nothing executes until you confirm.

You can also modify what Command has staged before approving, so it’s not just a simple accept or reject.

Your data and privacy

Command is designed to use only what it needs in order to respond to your prompts.

Sensitive personal and account information — including card numbers, SSNs, dates of birth, and home addresses — is never sent to the underlying AI model. When Command needs to reference something less sensitive (but something we believe the model doesn’t need to know, like a recipient’s name, account balances, or the email addresses of users on an account) we send an internal reference ID and only surface the real data to you directly in Mercury’s interface.

Command authenticates through your existing Mercury session. This means it can only access data that a user is already authorized to see. Likewise, it can only perform actions that a user is already authorized to perform inside their Mercury account. For example, if a team member can’t view account balances in Mercury, they can’t ask Command to surface them either.

Mercury Command is powered by third-party AI providers. In order to generate responses, some data is shared with these providers, but your conversations are never used to train their models.

Using Command is optional. You’re never required to use Command. Your core Mercury experience — payments, accounts, and cards — works the same as always whether you choose to use it or not.

Getting started

Command is available to all Mercury business and personal customers. You’ll find it in the bottom left corner of your Mercury dashboard.

Here are some prompts to get you started:

  • “How did our cash position change this month?”
  • “Show me software spend by vendor.”
  • “Find the wire details for our operating account.”
  • “Generate a custom bank letter for this account.”
  • “Show me all uncategorized transactions from April.”
  • “Create an invoice for [existing customer] for [amount].”
  • “Prepare an ACH payment to [recipient] for [amount].”
  • “Set up an auto-transfer rule to keep $25,000 in our operating account.”
  • “Show me card activity for employee this month.”
  • “Freeze the card ending [1234] until I review the charge.”
  • “Set a monthly spending limit for this card.”
  • “Invite [name, email] and assign the right role for a bookkeeper.”
  • “Summarize what needs my attention before month end.”
  • “Turn Mercury to dark mode.”
  • “How much interest have I earned on my savings this year?”
  • “Create a virtual card for my Netflix subscription with a $15 limit.”
  • “Move $1,000 from my business account to personal.”

If you’re a user on a Mercury Business account, you may be eligible to have your Mercury Personal annual subscription fee waived. This article explains who qualifies, how long the waiver lasts, and what happens if your eligibility changes.

Who is eligible?

You may be eligible for the subscription fee waiver if all of the following are true:

  • You apply for and open a Mercury Personal account, agree to the terms of use and customer agreements, and remain in good standing

A “Mercury Business user” is an individual who has been added as a team member on a Mercury Business account and assigned a role (such as Admin, Teammate, or a Custom role with defined permissions).

Your Mercury Personal subscription fee is waived as long as you continue to:

  • Be a user on a Mercury Business account
  • Remain on a Business account that is active and in good standing
  • Mercury continues to offer this fee waiver

There is no separate action required to maintain the benefit while you remain eligible. Mercury may modify, suspend, or discontinue this benefit at any time. If the offering changes and the subscription fee is reinstated, you’ll receive advance notice and have the option to cancel your Mercury Personal account before being charged the annual renewal fee.

What happens if my Business account status changes?

You may lose the subscription fee waiver if:

Personal: Invest

Managing your investments

Once you transfer funds into your Invest account, we automatically invest them based on your portfolio’s target allocation. You can track your balance, activity, and returns from the Invest dashboard. You can also deposit or withdraw funds at any time.

If your financial situation changes, we recommend reviewing your portfolio allocation to ensure it still fits your goals.

Maintaining your target allocation

As the market fluctuates, your portfolio may drift from its original allocation. For example, if your target is 60% stocks and 40% treasuries, market gains might shift it to 65% stocks and 35% treasuries.

We aim to keep your portfolio close to its target by rebalancing strategically – especially when:

  • You deposit or withdraw money
  • Your portfolio receives dividends

Here’s how it works:

  • When you deposit funds or receive dividends, we buy more of the underweight assets (those below your target).
  • When you withdraw funds, we sell more of the overweight assets (those above your target).

Example:

Your target: 60% stocks / 40% treasuries Current: 65% stocks / 35% treasuries

  • If you deposit $1,000, we’ll invest more in treasuries to correct the imbalance.
  • If you withdraw $1,000, we’ll sell more stocks since they’re over their target weight.

This ongoing approach helps nudge your portfolio back toward your target—without triggering unnecessary taxes.

Note: Withdrawals may have tax implications.

How do you minimize taxes when selling investments?

Whenever we sell shares (for a withdrawal or rebalancing), we use a method called tax lot optimization. This means:

  • We prioritize selling shares with losses first (to offset gains).
  • If we must sell gains, we prefer long-term holdings (typically taxed at lower rates).

This balances reducing your overall tax burden while keeping your portfolio aligned with your goals.

Can I change my portfolio allocation?

Yes. You can adjust your portfolio allocation anytime from your Invest page by clicking Edit Portfolio. For even more custom allocations not listed, email us at personal@mercury.com and we will gladly help you make changes.

How do I track investment performance?

You can track your returns from the Performance section of your dashboard. You’ll see returns for:

  • The past week
  • The past month
  • All-time (since you started investing)

How does Mercury calculate my performance?

We use a simple return calculation to show how much your money has grown compared to how much you’ve invested.

This approach:

  • Calculates the change in your account value over time
  • Accounts for deposits and withdrawals
  • Presents your return as a percentage gain or loss

Example:

  • You invest $10,000
  • Later, you add $5,000 (total contributions = $15,000)
  • Your account is now worth $16,500
  • Gain = $1,500 → Simple return = 10% ($1,500 / $15,000 = 0.10 or 10%)

You can view your simple return in the Performance section of your dashboard.

How do I access tax documents for my investment account?

If your Investment Account had certain taxable activity – like dividends or investment sales – you’ll receive a Consolidated Form 1099. This includes:

  • Form 1099-DIV – for any dividends paid to your account
  • Form 1099-B – for any sales of securities

If your account didn’t have any dividends or sales during the year, you won’t receive a tax form.

You’ll be able to access these tax documents from your Settings > Documents page.

Open, fund, and withdraw from a Mercury Personal investment account

Investment accounts are brokerage accounts that let you invest directly from your Mercury Personal account into a portfolio of carefully selected Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs).

Eligibility requirements

  • U.S. citizen or permanent resident or
  • Visa holder with one of the following unexpired visas:

How to apply

  • Complete a short questionnaire to help us understand your risk profile
  • Review your recommended portfolio
  • Accept the required disclosures and agreements

Most applications are automatically approved. If we need more time, we’ll follow up within a few business days.

What can I invest in?

Mercury Personal offers several portfolio options based on your investment goals and risk preferences. During the application, we’ll ask you a few questions and recommend a portfolio that fits your needs. You can change your selection at any time.

Depending on your portfolio, your investments may include one or both of these ETFs:

iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (SGOV)

  • Invests in short-term U.S. Treasury bills
  • Designed for capital preservation and stable income generation
  • View prospectus

Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI)

  • Provides diversified exposure to thousands of U.S. stocks
  • Designed for long-term growth potential
  • View prospectus

Note: Past performance does not guarantee future results. All investments involve risk and potential for loss.

How do deposits and withdrawals work?

Deposits: When you add money into your Investment Account, its automatically invested based on your selected portfolio allocation. Deposits that arrive before market close are typically invested the same day;those made after market close are processed the next business day.

Withdrawals: When you withdraw money, we sell your investments based on your current portfolio allocation. After the sale, it typically takes 1-3 business days for the funds to settle and appear in your account.

What fees are associated with Investment Accounts?

Mercury charges a low advisory fee of 0.10% per year (10 basis points) on the assets in your investment account.

  • The fee is accrued daily and charged monthly.
  • It’s automatically deducted from your account at the beginning of the next month.

Example:

If you invest $50,000 on March 10th, your fee would be about $3.01 based on 22 days of management, and assuming the net market value of your assets remains constant at $50,000 during this period

  • Daily fee rate: (0.10% / 365) = 0.00000274 (or 0.000274%)
  • Fee calculation: (Daily fee rate) × (Daily Asset value) × (Number of days managed)
  • March fee: (0.10% / 365) × $50,000 × 22 = $3.01

Note: The underlying ETFs in your portfolio (like SGOV and VTI) also have built-in fees commonly referred to as “expense ratios”. These are included in the fund’s price – not charged separately.

Is there a minimum deposit required to get started?

Nope. There’s no minimum to open or fund your Investment Account. We will take advantage of fractional shares to invest available funds according to your selected portfolio allocation.

Do you offer trust or retirement accounts or (eg IRA, Roth, 529)?

We only offer Individual and Joint brokerage accounts at this time. If you are interested in other types of accounts, please let us know at personal@mercury.com. Your feedback helps us shape what we build next.

How do you protect my money?

Your Investment Account is:
  • Advised by Mercury Advisory LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser (“Mercury Advisory”)
  • Custodied by Apex Clearing Corporation, our investment partner and a registered broker dealer and member FINRA / SIPC
SIPC Protection:

Your investments are protected by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC):

  • Up to $500,000, including $250,000 uninvested cash
  • Covers missing securities in the rare case of fraud or broker failure
  • Does not cover market losses

Learn more at sipc.org. Investment accounts are not FDIC insured.
